newsitem.title: USA: Senate poised to act on last of S&L crisis.
newsitem.headline: Senate poised to act on last of S&L crisis.

text.p: The Senate was poised to pass legislation Monday putting to rest the lingering hangover of the savings and loan crisis.
The House passed the measure Saturday as part of a broader budget bill that is now in the hands of the Senate, where a vote was expected late in the day.
"It looks like today will be the day it gets through the Senate," Treasury Undersecretary John Hawke said.
The Clinton Administration has endorsed the banking measure aimed at beefing-up the undercapitalized Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF), which insures deposits at thrifts.

Regulators had warned of a potential default on Financing Corp. (FICO) bonds, issued in the late 1980s to help with clean-up costs for hundreds of failed thrifts, if steps were not taken to bolster the thrift fund.
"We are enormously pleased that the last vestiges of the problems with the thrift industry have now been solved," without using taxpayer funds, Hawke said.
A portion of the premiums that thrifts pay to the SAIF is used to make annual interest payments on the FICO bonds.

The banking measure would require the thrift industry to pay a one-time charge of $4.7 billion to boost the SAIF, after which thrifts and banks would share the $793 million in annual FICO interest payments.
Banks viewed the measure as an unwarranted "tax" on their industry and would have opposed it if other provisions had not been added such as regulatory relief and lender liability.

The lender liability provision would exempt financial institutions from liability if they foreclosed on properties involving hazardous materials, as long as the lender was not involved in managing the property.
A compromise was worked out that satisfied some concerns of consumer groups that some of the regulatory relief measures would hurt consumers.
Insurance agents who had fought to tack on measures making it more difficult for banks to gain ground in insurance did not succeed in the bill that passed the House.
Although one provision that the insurance industry had sought was included -- that federal deposit insurance would not cover retirement certificates of deposit.

House Banking Committee Chairman James Leach, R-Iowa, over the weekend said the Republican leadership intended to address the concerns of the insurance agents in "comprehensive" financial industry reform in the next Congress.

Federal Reserve Gov. Susan Phillips said the Fed was disappointed that agreement was not reached this year on reform of the the Glass-Steagall Act, a Depression-era law that separates commercial and investment banking.
"We continue to believe that additional modernisation is needed," Phillips said.
